quote:
The task asks for the floor of the k-th root of a non-negative integer n: the largest non-negative r whose k-th power does not exceed n.

The submission handles zero up front and then climbs upward from zero one step at a time. The core of it is:

    if n == 0:
        return 0
    r = 0
    while (r + 1) ** k <= n:
        r += 1
    return r

The loop keeps incrementing r as long as the next candidate, raised to the k-th power, still fits under n. When it stops, r satisfies r**k <= n while (r+1)**k > n, which is exactly the definition in the specification. Nothing here refers to 8, 16 or 1, the values in the example calls; the stopping condition is written purely in terms of n and k.

To confirm generality I traced an input the examples leave out, integer_nth_root(26, 3). The loop accepts 1 (cube 1) and 2 (cube 8), then tries 3, whose cube is 27 and exceeds 26, so it returns 2. That is right, since 26 sits just below a perfect cube and the floor must drop to 2. For k = 1 it returns n itself, and for n = 1 with any exponent it returns 1, both consistent with the definition. Because it uses only integer arithmetic it stays exact for very large n, where a floating-point root could round the wrong way. The search is linear in the answer, so it would be slow for enormous inputs, but that affects speed rather than correctness, and the early zero check is redundant but harmless.

The submission keeps a set of every open-bracket count that some interpretation of the prefix so far could produce, starting from a set containing only zero. For an opening bracket, each count moves up by one. For a closing bracket, each positive count moves down by one, while a count of zero is dropped because closing would go negative. For a star, each count spawns three successors: one higher, one lower when that stays non-negative, and unchanged. The set is replaced after every character, the function gives up with False if the set ever empties, and at the end it answers whether zero is among the reachable counts.

That is a sound dynamic-programming approach. Refusing negative counts enforces that no prefix closes more than it has opened, and demanding zero at the end enforces that every opening bracket gets closed. Because stars contribute all three options, the set captures every achievable balance.

All three examples expect True, so I checked a False case outside them: a star, then a closing bracket, then an opening bracket. After the star the reachable counts are zero and one. The closing bracket turns one into zero and discards zero, leaving just zero. The final opening bracket leaves only one, so zero is absent and the function returns False. That is correct, because a trailing opening bracket can never be matched. The set never grows beyond the string length, so the cost is quadratic at worst.

The submission converts everything to minutes and floor-divides by the length of a day:

    days = total_minutes // 1440
    return days

Adding the departure offset to the duration gives the arrival time measured from the midnight at the start of the departure day. Dividing that by 1440, the number of minutes in a day, and discarding the remainder counts how many full day boundaries lie between that starting midnight and arrival, which is exactly the number of midnights crossed. Because both inputs are non-negative, the result cannot be negative.

A useful untested boundary is arrival_date_offset(23, 30, 30). Departure is 1410 minutes after midnight; adding 30 gives exactly 1440, and 1440 // 1440 is 1. Arriving at 00:00 the next day means one midnight has been reached, so 1 is correct. By contrast arrival_date_offset(23, 30, 29) gives 1439 // 1440 = 0, arriving at 23:59 on the same day. A long flight, say departure at 20:00 with a duration of 3000 minutes, gives (1200 + 3000) // 1440 = 2, arriving at 22:00 two days later. None of the arithmetic depends on the example values; the formula is general and needs no special handling for any duration.
